newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian tensions seen leading to more unrest.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian tensions seen leading to more unrest.

text.p: Two riots in two weeks in Indonesia illustrate that ethnic and religious tensions among the country's 200 million people are ready to explode, social and political analysts said on Sunday.
"Indonesia is like a dangerous volcano," Tjipta Lesmana, a lecturer at the state University of Indonesia, told Reuters.

He said economic disparity and social animosity between various groups had combined with resentment of the authorities to trigger the recent unrest and show that people were becoming increasingly disenchanted with authoritarian rule.
"I believe riots will continue and this is the government's own fault," Lesman said.
Sociologist Arief Budiman said the violence indicated people no longer viewed the government, police and courts as just.
"What they can do is to unite, and the most effective way is to unite through religion and ethnic roots," he said.

Five people were killed, nine were injured and dozens of homes were burned during tribal rioting in West Kalimantan province on Borneo island last week, sparked by a fight over a woman at a music concert.

The previous week, a mob of mainly Moslem youths set buildings and churches ablaze in the West Java town of Tasikmalaya, apparently incensed by a report of police brutality towards some Moslem religious teachers. Four people, including two ethnic Chinese, died in the riots. "These problems will not happen if the government acts wisely. They will not happen if, for instance, labourers have the right to make their demand or people evicted from their homes can seek justice in court or seek help from the police," Budiman said.
The Kalimantan riot erupted after a man from Madura island off Java reportedly stabbed two native Borneo Dayak tribesmen in a row over a woman.
More than 5,000 people of the Maduran ethnic group, who moved to Kalimantan on a government resettlement programme, fled the riot area to safety.
In a New Year address, President Suharto called for tolerance and unity and pledged more openness and democracy.
Lesmana said he agreed with Suharto's call, but added that words were not enough.
"The government should come up with real action to prevent disturbances recurring. For example, they should punish the people involved in the (West Java) riots," he said.
Budiman said the growing gap between the rich and poor had fueled ethnic and religious conflict.
Moslems, who constitute more than 80 percent of the population, have felt marginalised by the country's rapid economic development.

The economy's growth has disproportionately benefited the more affluent Chinese and Christians, who tended to become targets of violence in disturbances that grew out of relatively insignificant incidents.

In October, a Moslem mob in Situbondo in East Java burned 25 churches as well as other buildings in a rampage sparked by the trial of a Moslem heretic who was subsequently jailed for blasphemy. Five Christians died in one blazing church.

Jakarta itself was hit by its worst riots in two decades on July 27 in violence sparked by factional infighting in the minority Indonesian Democratic Party in which the government had backed the ouster of the party's leader.
Lesmana blamed the disturbances on what he said were repressive government policies.
"People don't dare to say anything because of repression. The most obvious repression is what happened on July 27," he said.
